title: 1930s–1950s: Universal Monsters
thematicFocus: Gothic escapism, romanticized monsters, external threats.
culturalContext: Born during the Great Depression and World War II, horror allowed audiences to project their real-world anxieties onto fantastical, distant creatures (vampires, corpses, sea beasts). Monsters were symbolic and physically distinct from 'normal' human society. Fear of nuclear war and annihilation led to anxieties that were reflected in films like Godzilla and King Kong.

title: 1960s–1970s: Psychological Shift
thematicFocus: Real-world violence, domestic terror, loss of institutional trust.
culturalContext: Civil rights unrest, the Vietnam War, and the decay of the suburban nuclear family brought terror into domestic spaces (Psycho, Night of the Living Dead, The Texas Chain Saw Massacre). The monster was no longer a creature in a castle, but a neighbor or masked killer. The Exorcist and Carrie touched on anxieties surrounding female autonomy over their body during women's rights movements.

title: 1980s: Slasher Boom & The Satanic Panic
thematicFocus: Franchise morality plays, practical gore, censorship, and moral panic.
culturalContext: The rise of home video (VHS) led to greater horror consumption, fueling mass-market slasher franchises (Friday the 13th, A Nightmare on Elm Street). Conservative social movements and the 'Satanic Panic' attempted to censor horror, resulting in heavily edited theatrical cuts and campier, formulaic sequels.

title: 1990s: Postmodern Revival
culturalContext: After the over-saturation of 80s sequels, horror started to become self-conscious. Scream and Wes Craven's New Nightmare started to break and deconstruct the supposed rules of the genre for a new generation that grew up watching slasher films.

title: 2000s: Extreme Realism & Torture Cinema
thematicFocus: Visceral vulnerability, post-9/11 anxiety, surveillance, and body horror.
culturalContext: Post-9/11 sociopolitical anxiety and 24-hour news coverage fueled uncompromising, claustrophobic violence (Saw, Hostel) alongside techno-dread remakes of Asian horror (The Ring). Fear shifted from specific masked killers to feeling trapped and helpless against institutions and physical suffering.

title: 2010s–Present: Blockbuster Haunted Houses & Elevated Horror
thematicFocus: Mainstream cinematic universes vs. grief, trauma, and auteur dread.
culturalContext: The modern era split into two distinct models: studio-driven, jump-scare 'haunted house' franchises (The Conjuring) for mass audiences, and indie 'elevated/auteur horror' (Hereditary, Midsommar, Get Out) that uses horror conventions to explore grief, generational trauma, social inequality, and psychological decay.
